items.new: But it was not only on this particular night that Ahab pondered over his charts alone in his cabin. Almost every night they were brought out. Almost every night some pencil marks were erased and others substituted. For with the charts of all four oceans spread before him, Ahab was threading a maze of currents and eddies, all with a view to the more certain accomplishment of that monomaniac thought of his soul.

items.new: There was a circumstance that at first glance seemed to entangle his delirious but still methodical scheme. But perhaps it did not in reality. Though the gregarious sperm whales have their regular seasons for particular grounds, you generally cannot conclude that the herds that haunted such-and-such a latitude or longitude this year, say, will turn out to be identically the same as those found there the season before — though there are peculiar and unquestionable cases where the contrary has proved true. In general, the same remark applies, only within narrower limits, to the solitaries and hermits among the mature, aged sperm whales. So although Moby Dick had in a former year been seen, for example, on what is called the Seychelle ground in the Indian Ocean, or in Volcano Bay on the Japanese coast, it did not follow that if the Pequod visited either of those spots at any later corresponding season, she would infallibly meet him there. The same was true of some other feeding-grounds where he had at times shown himself. But all these seemed only his casual stopping-places and ocean-inns, so to speak, not his places of long residence. And where Ahab's chances of achieving his object have been spoken of so far, the reference has only been to whatever wayside, preliminary, extra prospects were his before a particular fixed time or place was reached — when all possibilities would become probabilities, and, as Ahab fondly thought, every possibility the next thing to a certainty. That particular time and place were joined in the one technical phrase: the Season-on-the-Line (the Line being the equator). For there and then, for several consecutive years, Moby Dick had been periodically sighted, lingering in those waters for a while, just as the sun in its annual round loiters for a predicted interval in any one sign of the Zodiac. It was there, too, that most of the deadly encounters with the white whale had taken place; there the very waves were storied with his deeds; there also was that tragic spot where the monomaniac old man had found the awful motive for his vengeance. But with the cautious thoroughness and unresting vigilance with which Ahab threw his brooding soul into this unfaltering hunt, he would not allow himself to rest all his hopes on the one crowning fact just mentioned, however flattering it might be to those hopes; nor, in the sleeplessness of his vow, could he so calm his unquiet heart as to put off all searching in the meantime.

items.new: Now, the Pequod had sailed from Nantucket at the very beginning of the Season-on-the-Line. No possible effort could have enabled her commander to make the great passage southward, round Cape Horn, and then, running down sixty degrees of latitude, arrive in the equatorial Pacific in time to cruise there. Therefore he had to wait for the next season. Yet the premature hour of the Pequod's sailing had perhaps been correctly chosen by Ahab with a view to this very state of things. For an interval of three hundred and sixty-five days and nights lay before him — an interval which, instead of enduring it impatiently ashore, he would spend in a miscellaneous hunt, in case the White Whale, spending his vacation in seas far from his periodical feeding-grounds, should by chance turn up his wrinkled brow off the Persian Gulf, or in the Bengal Bay, or the China Seas, or in any other waters haunted by his race. So Monsoons, Pampas, Nor'-Westers, Harmattans, Trades — any wind but the Levanter and the Simoon — might blow Moby Dick into the devious zigzag world-circle of the Pequod's circumnavigating wake.

items.new: Often, when he was driven from his hammock by exhausting and intolerably vivid dreams of the night — dreams which took up his own intense thoughts of the day and carried them on amid a clash of frenzies, whirling them round and round and round in his blazing brain until the very throbbing of his life-spot became unbearable anguish — and when, as was sometimes the case, these spiritual throes heaved his being up from its foundations, and a chasm seemed to open in him, from which forked flames and lightnings shot up, and accursed fiends beckoned him to leap down among them — when this hell within him yawned beneath him, a wild cry would be heard through the ship, and with glaring eyes Ahab would burst from his stateroom, as though escaping from a bed that was on fire. Yet these outbursts, perhaps, instead of being the irrepressible symptoms of some hidden weakness, or of fright at his own resolve, were only the plainest signs of its intensity. For at such times crazy Ahab, the scheming, unappeasably steadfast hunter of the white whale — this Ahab who had gone to his hammock — was not the agent that made him burst from it again in horror. That agent was the eternal, living principle, or soul, in him; and in sleep, being for the time separated from the characterizing mind, which at other times used it as its outer vehicle or agent, it spontaneously sought to escape from the scorching nearness of the frantic thing of which, for the time, it was no longer an integral part. But since the mind does not exist unless joined with the soul, it must have been that in Ahab's case, as he yielded up all his thoughts and fancies to his one supreme purpose, that purpose, by the sheer stubbornness of its own will, forced itself, against gods and devils, into a kind of self-assumed, independent being of its own. Indeed, it could grimly live and burn while the common vitality to which it was joined fled horror-stricken from the unbidden and unfathered birth. Therefore the tormented spirit that glared out of bodily eyes, when what seemed Ahab rushed from his room, was for the time only an emptied thing, a formless sleepwalking being — a ray of living light, to be sure, but without an object to color, and therefore a blankness in itself. God help you, old man, your thoughts have created a creature in you; and whoever's intense thinking thus makes him a Prometheus has a vulture feeding upon his heart forever — and that vulture is the very creature he creates.

items.new: But not only did each of these famous whales enjoy great individual celebrity — indeed, you may call it ocean-wide renown; not only was he famous in life and is now immortal in forecastle stories after death; but he was admitted into all the rights, privileges, and distinctions of a name, and had as much of a name, in fact, as Cambyses or Caesar. Was it not so, O Timor Tom! you famous leviathan, scarred like an iceberg, who lurked so long in the Oriental straits of that name, whose spout was often seen from the palmy beach of Ombay? Was it not so, O New Zealand Jack! you terror of all cruisers that crossed their wakes in the neighborhood of the Tattoo Land? Was it not so, O Morquan! King of Japan, whose lofty jet, they say, at times took on the likeness of a snow-white cross against the sky? Was it not so, O Don Miguel! you Chilean whale, marked like an old tortoise with mystic hieroglyphics upon your back! In plain prose, here are four whales as well known to students of Cetacean History as Marius or Sylla to the classical scholar.

items.new: To accomplish his object Ahab had to use tools; and of all tools used in the shadow of the moon, men are the most apt to get out of order. He knew, for example, that however magnetic his ascendancy over Starbuck was in some respects, that ascendancy did not cover the whole spiritual man, any more than mere bodily superiority implies intellectual mastery; for to the purely spiritual, the intellectual stands only in a sort of bodily relation. Starbuck's body and Starbuck's coerced will were Ahab's, so long as Ahab kept his magnet at Starbuck's brain; still, he knew that for all this the chief mate in his soul abhorred his captain's quest, and if he could, would joyfully cut himself loose from it, or even thwart it. It might be a long time before the White Whale was seen. During that long interval Starbuck would always be liable to fall into open relapses of rebellion against his captain's leadership, unless some ordinary, prudential, circumstantial influences were brought to bear on him. Not only that, but the subtle insanity of Ahab concerning Moby Dick was nowhere more significantly shown than in his superlative sense and shrewdness in foreseeing that, for the present, the hunt should somehow be stripped of the strange imaginative impiety that naturally clothed it; that the full terror of the voyage must be kept back in the dim background (for few men's courage can hold out against long brooding unrelieved by action); and that when they stood their long night watches, his officers and men must have some nearer things to think about than Moby Dick. For however eagerly and impetuously the savage crew had hailed the announcement of his quest, all sailors of every sort are more or less capricious and unreliable — they live in the changing outer weather, and they breathe in its fickleness — and when they are kept at a long pursuit of some remote and blank object, however much it promises life and passion in the end, it is above all necessary that temporary interests and occupations should intervene and hold them healthily suspended for the final dash.

items.new: I was Queequeg's attendant, or page, while he was busy at the mat. As I kept passing the filling, or woof, of marline back and forth between the long yarns of the warp, using my own hand as the shuttle, and as Queequeg, standing sideways, every now and then slid his heavy oaken sword between the threads and, idly looking off at the water, carelessly and unthinkingly drove every yarn home — I say, so strange a dreaminess reigned then over all the ship and all the sea, broken only by the intermittent dull sound of the sword, that it seemed as if this were the Loom of Time, and I myself a shuttle mechanically weaving and weaving away at the Fates. There lay the fixed threads of the warp, subject to only one single, ever-returning, unchanging vibration, and that vibration just enough to allow other threads to be interwoven crosswise with its own. This warp seemed necessity; and here, I thought, with my own hand I ply my own shuttle and weave my own destiny into these unalterable threads. Meanwhile Queequeg's impulsive, indifferent sword sometimes hit the woof slantwise, or crookedly, or strongly, or weakly, as the case might be, and by this difference in the concluding blow produced a corresponding contrast in the final look of the finished fabric. This savage's sword, I thought, which in the end shapes and fashions both warp and woof — this easy, indifferent sword must be chance — yes, chance, free will, and necessity, in no way incompatible, all working together, interwoven. The straight warp of necessity, not to be swerved from its ultimate course — its every alternating vibration, indeed, only tending toward that; free will, still free to ply her shuttle between given threads; and chance, though restrained in its play within the straight lines of necessity, and directed sideways in its motions by free will — though thus hemmed in by both, chance rules each of them by turns, and strikes the last, shaping blow at events.

items.new: The ship was now kept away from the wind, and she went gently rolling before it. Since Tashtego reported that the whales had gone down heading to leeward, we confidently expected to see them again directly ahead of our bows. For that singular cunning the Sperm Whale at times shows — when, sounding (diving deep) with his head in one direction, he nevertheless mills round while hidden beneath the surface and swiftly swims off the opposite way — this deceitfulness of his could not be at work now; for there was no reason to suppose that the fish Tashtego had seen had been alarmed in any way, or indeed knew we were anywhere near. One of the men chosen as shipkeepers — that is, those not assigned to the boats — had by this time relieved the Indian at the mainmast head. The sailors at the fore and mizzen had come down; the line tubs were fixed in their places; the cranes were thrust out; the mainyard was backed; and the three boats swung over the sea like three samphire baskets over high cliffs. Outside the bulwarks their eager crews clung to the rail with one hand, while one foot was poised expectantly on the gunwale. That is how the long line of a man-of-war's men looks when they are about to throw themselves aboard an enemy's ship.
